item.title: Supermarket Fridge Cyberattacks in Europe: How to Secure OT and IoT Devices
item.description: Refrigerators in European supermarkets were remotely heated in October and November 2026. What is known so far, why a fridge controller is reachable at all, and seven measures to secure OT and IoT devices in retail and SMB networks.
item.content:encoded:
In October and November 2026, refrigerators and freezers in supermarkets across Europe were switched to temperatures that destroyed the food inside them. Nobody touched the devices physically. This article summarizes what is publicly known, explains why a refrigeration controller can be attacked over a network in the first place, and lists the measures that would have made such an attack much harder.

Status: This is based on media reports and company statements up to 6 November 2026. The investigations are ongoing. Where something is not confirmed, I say so.

What Happened

  • France, 12 October 2026: Refrigerators in stores of Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix and Coopérative U were heated and food was spoiled. Intermarché’s parent company expected losses of several million euros.
  • 2 November 2026: A second wave hit around 75 stores in Belgium (including Delhaize, Carrefour, Intermarché, Spar and an IKEA store), 13 SuperValu stores in Ireland, ICA and Coop stores in Sweden, and companies in the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland. In Stockholm, a freezer was reportedly heated to 50 °C.
  • Common element: Some of the affected systems used refrigeration control software from Danfoss. According to Danfoss, the affected customers had not updated their software. Security researchers from Claroty had reported vulnerabilities in Danfoss refrigeration controllers in August, which Danfoss says it fixed with an update.
  • Mechanism: The Belgian refrigeration service company Sabcobel said the units were switched into defrost mode, and that a software update alone is not enough: physical modifications are needed as well.

Not confirmed so far: how the attackers got access, whether the vulnerabilities reported in August were exploited, and who is behind the attacks. Belgium’s federal prosecutor has opened an investigation. The EU agriculture commissioner called the attacks a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.

Why Is a Fridge on the Network at All?

Commercial refrigeration is not a household fridge. A supermarket runs dozens of cooling units that are controlled centrally: temperatures, defrost cycles, alarms and energy optimization. The service company needs to see alarms at night and adjust settings without driving to the store.

That is a legitimate need. The problem is how it is often solved:

  • The controller or its web interface is reachable directly from the internet, sometimes with a port forward that someone set up years ago.
  • It sits in the same network as the cash registers, the office PCs and the guest Wi-Fi.
  • The service company uses a permanent remote access tool that nobody monitors.
  • The software has not been updated since installation, because “it works”.
  • Default passwords were never changed.

None of these is specific to refrigeration. The same pattern exists for building automation, heating and ventilation, access control, cameras, PV inverters and production machines. That is why this incident matters beyond supermarkets.

Seven Measures to Secure OT and IoT Devices

1. Know What You Have

You cannot protect devices you do not know about. Keep an inventory of every connected controller, gateway and sensor: vendor, model, software version, IP address, who manages it and how it is accessed remotely.

2. No Direct Exposure to the Internet

A management interface of an OT device should never be reachable from the internet. Check your firewall for port forwards and search for your public IP addresses in services such as Shodan to see what the outside world can reach.

3. Segment the Network

Put OT and IoT devices into their own VLAN or network segment. The firewall between the segments decides what may talk to what:

  • The refrigeration controller talks only to its management server and to the vendor’s cloud, if one is used.
  • Cash registers, office PCs and guest Wi-Fi cannot reach the controller at all.

More on segmentation in industrial networks: OT Networks: What an IT Engineer Actually Encounters on the Factory Floor.

4. Restrict Outbound Traffic

Many devices only need to reach a handful of destinations. Allow exactly those addresses and ports and block everything else. If a device is compromised, it cannot download tools or reach an attacker’s server.

5. Secure Remote Access for Vendors

The service company needs access, but on your terms:

  • Access through IPsec VPN or ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) with multi-factor authentication, never through an open port.
  • Access only to the systems the vendor maintains, not to the whole network.
  • Access enabled when needed and disabled afterwards, with logging of who connected when.

6. Updates and Credentials

Plan software updates for OT devices like you do for servers, coordinated with the vendor. Change all default passwords and use individual accounts instead of one shared login.

7. Safety Limits That Software Cannot Override

This is the lesson most specific to this incident. If a hacked controller can heat a freezer to 50 °C, the system has no independent safety limit. Physical or hardware-based limits and local alarms that work without the network ensure that a compromised controller cannot cause physical damage. Monitoring helps as well: unusual temperature changes or configuration changes at 3 a.m. should trigger an alarm immediately.

Quick Checklist for Small Businesses

  • Do we know which devices in our store are connected to the network?
  • Can any of them be reached from the internet?
  • Are they in a separate network from cash registers and guest Wi-Fi?
  • How does our service company connect, and can we see when it does?
  • When was the software last updated? Have the default passwords been changed?
  • Is there an alarm that works even if the network or the controller is down?

If you cannot answer one of these questions, that is where to start.

item.title: 🛡️ Visibility and Security Strategy in Enterprise Networks: Network Packet Broker (NPB) Masterclass
item.description: Strategic guide for traffic management, cybersecurity, and end-to-end visibility in enterprise networks. What is NPB? How to manage it with NIAC principles?
item.content:encoded:
In today’s enterprise network architectures, “speed” is no longer the sole criterion for success. The real challenge is knowing what flows within tens of gigabits of data traffic per second, ensuring security, and monitoring performance end-to-end. As the “intelligent traffic conductor” of modern networks, the Network Packet Broker (NPB) has become a strategic necessity for everything from cybersecurity to business continuity.

For the broader architecture context behind visibility strategy, see: IT Infrastructure Is Not a Collection of Products

1. Micro-Second Precision: End of Packet Loss (Buffering & Time-Stamping)

Network traffic does not always flow linearly; instantaneous bursts occur. While many standard switches drop packets during these bursts, a professional NPB solves this problem at the hardware level:

  • 500 ms Buffer Memory: NPB holds traffic momentarily in its memory, reducing packet loss to 0% during times when your analysis tools (DLP, IDS, Sniffer) cannot keep up with the speed. This is vital for forensics and debugging processes.
  • Hardware Time-Stamping: When performing latency analysis, “about an hour” is not a professional answer. With the hardware Time-Stamping feature offered by NPBs, you can stamp every packet with micro-second precision the moment it enters the system. These stamps are life-savers, especially in forensic analysis processes.

2. Intelligent Filtering and Protocol Mastery (L2-L4)

While L2-4 filtering (MAC, IP, Port) exists in many devices, the difference with an NPB is that it performs this process at “wire-speed” without compromising packet integrity and with unparalleled flexibility:

  • Flow Aggregation & Deduplication: It analyzes thousands of flows coming from massive 100 GB inputs, cleans duplicate packets (Deduplication), and converts all this chaos into a single optimized flow for analysis devices. Cleaning duplicate packets reduces the CPU load of your analysis devices by 30-50%.
  • Packet Slicing (Lighten the Load): You don’t always need to be in love with the entire packet. If your analysis tool only needs header information, perform Packet Slicing on the NPB to trim the payload. This way, you don’t overwhelm the disks and processors of your analysis devices with unnecessary data, gaining 100% efficiency.

3. Flexible Delivery Methods: Getting Traffic to the Target

NPB offers a rich “packaging” menu to deliver your filtered traffic to the analysis device:

  • ERSPAN & VXLAN/GRE Tunneling: It carries traffic to remote data centers or cloud-based analysis centers by encapsulating it over Layer 3 networks.
  • VLAN Tagging / Stripping: It adds tags for the analysis device to recognize the traffic or cleans these tags to lighten the load on the device.
  • Load Balancing: It distributes dense 100G traffic equally to 10G capacity analysis devices without breaking “session stickiness” (session integrity).

4. API Support, Automation, and the NIAC Vision

Manual intervention is a risk in modern IT operations. The automation capabilities offered by NPB provide agility to teams. However, do not view the process as just a simple “backup”; we integrate these devices into Network Infrastructure as Code (NIAC) principles thanks to Rest-API support.

  • NIAC & Disaster Recovery (DR): All critical filtering rules and port configurations on the device should be managed with NIAC principles. In the event of a hardware failure, we can migrate the entire architecture to a new device in seconds using automation scripts rather than manual configuration.
  • ITSM and SIEM Integration: During a cyber incident, filters can be automatically created via SIEM tools, or existing filters can be edited via API according to the instantaneous situation.

5. Performance and Security (Riverbed, DLP & SSL Offloading)

NPB is like a central “Data Hub” feeding all kinds of analysis devices on the network:

  • Network TAP (Inline Data Collection): It can receive traffic directly from cables going to servers (Network TAP), not just switch ports. This allows you to reach the “purest” data without affecting main traffic.
  • SSL/TLS Offloading: Don’t exhaust the CPUs of your Firewall or IPS devices with decryption. Handle this load on the NPB and send “clean” and unencrypted traffic to analysis devices. Let your security devices do their actual job; let the NPB handle the heavy lifting of decryption.
  • Riverbed Integration: By feeding NPM devices like Riverbed with the most accurate data, it detects application latencies and bottlenecks.
  • Call Centers (VoIP): It processes voice traffic in parallel; while one copy goes to the recording system, the user continues the conversation without any delay.

6. Encrypted Traffic and Data Center (DC) Strategy

Although internet traffic is encrypted, “East-West” traffic flowing unencrypted within the data center for performance reasons is still the biggest opportunity. Using NPB at these strategic points where traffic is transparent and mirroring the data provides 100% visibility without incurring decryption costs.

7. Market Leaders

While Keysight (Ixia) and Gigamon set the standards for high-performance solutions; brands like Arista, Garland Technology, and Profitap are indispensable for enterprise networks with their flexible port structures and innovative delivery methods.

Conclusion

The seamless orchestration of traffic mirroring and analysis flows is the definitive proof of how a complex network operation can be rendered controllable. By leveraging NIAC (Network Infrastructure as Code) and robust API integrations, this architecture transforms from a static hardware setup into a dynamic, “living” security platform.

Such a framework ensures that critical data reaches security tools with zero loss and maximum optimization, granting operational teams full visibility and command over the network.
